caption_hook: South Dakota stacks fossil badlands, a cave-riddled limestone and the granite of Mount Rushmore.

layers.name: BRULE FORMATION
layers.what: Ash-rich muds laid down by rivers and wind built the pink and tan bands of Badlands National Park. Erosion strips the soft layers away at about an inch a year.
layers.bonus: Its fossils include saber-toothed cats, giant pigs and the sheep-like oreodonts.

layers.name: PIERRE SHALE
layers.what: A deep inland sea once covered the Great Plains, and this gray mud settled on its floor. It is packed with fossil mosasaurs, ammonites and giant clams.
layers.bonus: It is named for Fort Pierre, across the Missouri River from the state capital.

layers.name: SPEARFISH FORMATION
layers.hook: The red ring around the hills
layers.what: Red mudstone and gypsum from dry tidal flats now form a brick-red valley that rings the Black Hills. From the air, the circle is easy to spot. Red tidal-flat mud is what gives it that color.
layers.bonus: The Lakota call this valley the Race Track, after a legendary race around the hills.

layers.name: PAHASAPA LIMESTONE
layers.what: A warm, clear sea left this thick limestone full of shells and corals. Groundwater later dissolved it into some of the longest caves in the world. Tours there run through twisting tunnels.
layers.bonus: Wind Cave and Jewel Cave both formed in it, each with well over 100 miles of passages.

layers.name: HARNEY PEAK GRANITE
layers.what: Molten rock cooled deep underground into a pale, hard granite, then rose with the Black Hills. It makes the spires of the Needles and the state's highest summit.
layers.bonus: Mount Rushmore is carved from it and wears away only about an inch per 10,000 years.
